interview_metadata.name: Mariella Sanchez
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Santa Ana and grew up in Fountain Valley in a Mexican-American family where Spanish was what we used at home and food was kind of how everybody showed love. My parents worked a lot, so from when I was little I learned to help out, be polite to elders, and make people feel welcome, which is honestly a big part of why I ended up in hospitality. As a kid I liked drawing, tagging along on family errands, and paying attention to places—how they smelled, how people talked, what made them feel warm or awkward. School was okay for me, but after the pandemic everything got more scattered, and by the time I was in high school I was juggling family stress, work, and feeling like the normal school path wasn't fitting me well anymore. I left before finishing and started working front-of-house at a café-restaurant, and what I thought would be a temporary job ended up becoming something I'm actually proud of because I'm good with people, reservations, and staying calm when things get hectic. Right now I still live with my parents and younger brother, I'm working as a hostess, and I recently started adult high school completion classes through a community college program because I do want to finish. My family is really important to me, and I don't have kids or a husband or anything like that, but I have a close circle of friends, coworkers, cousins, and people from yoga and running. A couple of big things that shaped me were the pandemic years, stepping away from regular high school, taking work seriously earlier than I expected, and traveling a little—like going to Guatemala and later a very budget trip to Kyoto—which made me think bigger about art, coffee, and what I want my future to look like. Now my goal is to finish school, move up to lead hostess and eventually floor manager, and one day open a café-gallery space that feels creative and welcoming.

follow_ups.question: What was your home life like when you were little?
follow_ups.response: Busy, loving, and loud in a good way—my mom was always cooking or getting ready for work, my dad was fixing something, and weekends usually meant family, church holidays, or visiting relatives.

follow_ups.question: When did art and coffee become such a big part of your life?
follow_ups.response: Drawing started when I was a kid, but coffee got serious once I worked around it and started tasting it more intentionally, writing notes, and visiting local coffee spots.

follow_ups.question: How does your life now feel different from what you expected as a younger teenager?
follow_ups.response: I thought I'd be in a more typical college path by now, but instead I've become more practical and independent sooner, and I think that changed me in a good way too.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yeah, for me the crossroads was when I stopped the normal high school track and started working seriously. My family was under a lot of pressure after the pandemic years—money felt tighter, everybody was tired, and I was struggling to stay focused in school in a way that felt meaningful. I got a front-of-house job thinking it would just help for a little while, but I realized pretty fast that I was good at handling people, switching between English and Spanish, and keeping things organized under pressure. At the time, part of me felt ashamed, like I was falling behind, because a lot of people my age were talking about graduation and college applications. But another part of me felt relief because I finally felt useful and competent, and over time I started seeing that this wasn't the end of anything, just a different route. Now I'm back in classes through an adult completion program, and I think that whole detour made me more grounded and clearer about what kind of work and life I want.

follow_ups.question: Do you remember the moment when it felt real that you were stepping off the regular school path?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, it was during my senior year when I realized I was missing assignments, feeling overwhelmed, and also counting on work money, and I kind of knew I couldn't keep pretending everything was fine.

follow_ups.question: What did your family say when you made that change?
follow_ups.response: They worried, but they weren't harsh about it; my parents mostly wanted me to be safe, working, and eventually come back to finish, which I am doing now.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was honestly both. The stress built up gradually, so in that sense it 'just happened,' but taking the job seriously and staying with it was definitely a conscious decision.

follow_ups.question: What made it feel like the right decision then?
follow_ups.response: I could immediately help with money and I felt more capable at work than I did sitting in classes I was falling behind in.

follow_ups.question: Do you still feel good about that choice now?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes, especially because I'm not stuck there mentally anymore—I'm finishing school, just on a different timeline.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes, I think a school counselor or a program that really explained flexible options earlier would have helped a lot. I didn't need someone to lecture me; I needed someone to say, 'Here are three realistic ways to finish, and here's how to do it while you work.'

follow_ups.question: Was there any support you did get that mattered?
follow_ups.response: My mom mattered, because even when she was worried she kept saying finishing later was still finishing.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have changed things the most?
follow_ups.response: Practical help—clear information, flexible class schedules, and somebody checking in before things got too far behind.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: The people I'm closest to are my parents and my younger brother. My mom, Elena, is the emotional center of the house—she's the one everybody talks to first, and she's also the person I cook with the most, especially when we make tamales or mole for family gatherings. My dad, Raul, is quieter but really dependable; we watch games together sometimes, and he has this way of showing care by fixing things or making sure my car tires have air. My brother Mateo is 15, and even though we annoy each other like normal siblings, I'm protective of him and help him with homework or just listen when school gets dramatic. My grandma Rosa doesn't live with us, but she's very important to me and we see her often. I don't have children, and I'm not living with a romantic partner or anything like that—I dated someone casually last year, but right now my life is more focused on work, school, and family.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk to first when something important happens?
follow_ups.response: Usually my mom first, and then my best friend if it's something I need to talk through from a different angle.

follow_ups.question: What does family time usually look like for you?
follow_ups.response: Sunday dinner is the most regular thing—someone cooks, my dad puts on a game or music, and we catch up even if everybody's tired.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: No, that's basically my immediate family. I also have a lot of cousins and aunts nearby, and in a Mexican family that can feel almost immediate too.

follow_ups.question: Is there one extended family member you're especially close to?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, my cousin Lupita—she's a little older than me and feels like an older sister sometimes.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see extended family?
follow_ups.response: Usually a couple times a month, more around birthdays, holidays, or if somebody is hosting a big meal.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yeah, definitely. My best friend Daniela and I have known each other since high school, and she's one of the few people who has seen every version of me—stressed, excited, messy, motivated, all of it. At work I'm close with a coworker named Jasmine, and we trade shifts sometimes, vent after hard rushes, and send each other coffee spots and art events. I also have people from yoga and the OC Striders running club who I don't tell everything to, but they keep me active and socially connected. And I go to open-mic nights sometimes, so there are a few creative people in that orbit too. I'm not in a serious relationship right now.

follow_ups.question: How often do you actually spend time with Daniela?
follow_ups.response: Usually at least once a week in person, and we text almost every day.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your friends usually do together?
follow_ups.response: Coffee shops, open-mic nights, beach walks, museum days, sometimes just watching the Dodgers or a movie and talking.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Fountain Valley, and it feels pretty suburban and steady. There are a lot of families, parks, strip malls, Vietnamese restaurants, Mexican spots, and it's close enough that I can get to the beach, Costa Mesa, or Santa Ana without it being a whole trip. I like that it's diverse without feeling super chaotic, and for everyday life it's convenient—groceries, coffee, errands, work routes, all that. It's not the most artsy place by itself, so when I want galleries or murals I usually drive out a bit. But for living, it feels grounded and familiar.

follow_ups.question: What places in the neighborhood do you use most often?
follow_ups.response: The grocery stores, our local park, a couple coffee shops, and the main roads that get me to work fast.

follow_ups.question: What do you like best about it?
follow_ups.response: That it feels calm and multicultural at the same time, and that my family network is all within a pretty easy drive.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe here. I'm still careful like any woman would be—especially if I'm coming home late from work—but I don't feel on edge in my neighborhood all the time.

follow_ups.question: Are there certain times you feel less safe?
follow_ups.response: Late at night in parking lots more than in the neighborhood itself.

follow_ups.question: What do you do to be careful?
follow_ups.response: I text when I'm leaving work, park in brighter areas, and keep my phone charged.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is stability, convenience, and being near family. The downside is it's expensive, pretty car-dependent, and if I want more culture or nightlife or art events, I usually have to go to Santa Ana, Costa Mesa, Laguna, or Long Beach.

follow_ups.question: Does the cost of living affect your decisions much?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, a lot—it affects how much I can save, whether I can move out, and how often I say yes to things.

follow_ups.question: Do you see yourself staying there long-term?
follow_ups.response: Not forever in the exact same setup, but I do see myself staying in Orange County for a while.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it's me, my mom Elena, my dad Raul, and my younger brother Mateo. We live in a rented apartment, and everybody has their own rhythm—my parents both work, Mateo is in school and soccer, and I juggle work and classes. I have my own corner of the room with my art stuff, coffee gear, and a couple houseplants I'm always promising to water on time. The house is busy but pretty loving, and there isn't anybody staying with us long-term right now.

follow_ups.question: Who do you spend the most time with inside the house?
follow_ups.response: Probably my mom in the kitchen and my brother in the evenings when he's doing homework or watching something.

follow_ups.question: How do household chores usually get split up?
follow_ups.response: My parents do the bigger stuff, but I help with dishes, cooking, grocery runs, and keeping shared spaces picked up.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone living there right now is a permanent member of the household.

follow_ups.question: So no one is just crashing there for a while?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it's been the same four of us for a while.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My grandma or a cousin might stay one night once in a while after a family event, but nobody stays regularly.

follow_ups.question: Who is the most common overnight visitor?
follow_ups.response: Usually my grandma if a family gathering runs late.

follow_ups.question: Is that frequent?
follow_ups.response: Not really, just every now and then.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone who usually lives there is currently home.

follow_ups.question: No one away at college or anything like that?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No one in the hospital or traveling long-term?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week changes depending on the schedule, but weekends are the most fixed because I usually work brunch shifts Saturday and Sunday, so those days start early. On weekdays I usually have two or three work shifts, plus my adult high school completion classes two evenings a week. If I have a free morning, I'll try to do yoga, go for a run, or hike if I can get out early enough. Sundays usually end with family dinner, and if there's a Dodgers or Lakers game on, my dad and brother will have that playing. So my week is a mix of work, school, trying to stay active, and helping at home.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually wake up on workdays?
follow_ups.response: If it's a brunch shift, around 6:00 or 6:30; if it's a later shift, more like 7:30 or 8:00.

follow_ups.question: When do you fit in homework?
follow_ups.response: Usually late evening after work if I still have energy, or on Tuesday mornings when I'm more clear-headed.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a hostess at a busy café-brunch restaurant in Costa Mesa. Most of my job is greeting people, managing the waitlist and reservations, coordinating seating with servers, answering questions, and jumping onto the POS or to-go orders when it gets slammed. My schedule changes week to week, but I usually work around 28 to 32 hours, with almost every Saturday and Sunday plus a few weekday shifts. Weekend shifts are morning to mid-afternoon, and weekday shifts can be afternoons into evening. It's very people-facing, very fast, and I actually like that.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually wear to work?
follow_ups.response: Mostly all black with comfortable shoes, my name tag, hair neat, and just a simple polished look because we're front-of-house.

follow_ups.question: What's the busiest part of your week there?
follow_ups.response: Weekend brunch by far—there are always people waiting, phones ringing, and everyone wanting a table at the same time.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: Yeah, outside of work and class I help around the house a lot. I do grocery runs with my mom, cook sometimes, help my brother with English or history homework, and drive my grandma to things occasionally if my schedule lines up. I also keep a coffee journal, sketch café scenes, and try to make one yoga class a week in Laguna Hills when I can afford the drop-in. Every so often I volunteer at local cultural festivals, especially if they're Latino community events.

follow_ups.question: What do you cook most often?
follow_ups.response: Weeknight basics mostly, but when I have time I love making tamales or working on my mole.

follow_ups.question: How often do you volunteer?
follow_ups.response: Not every week, but a few times a year around festival season or community events.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is starting my adult completion classes again, because now I have to be a lot more structured with my time. I've also been trying to cut back on random phone scrolling and use a calendar so I don't miss assignments or work things. Another shift is that I've been more intentional about exercise because when I'm stressed, I can either get really motivated or really scattered. So lately my routine is less drifting and more planning than it used to be.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been back in classes?
follow_ups.response: A few months now.

follow_ups.question: Has that change felt good or stressful?
follow_ups.response: Both, but mostly good because it makes me feel like I'm moving forward again.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I don't have children, so that's not part of my routine.

follow_ups.question: So no parenting responsibilities of your own?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with any younger relatives at all?
follow_ups.response: Just sometimes with my brother or little cousins, but not in a parent role.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: I haven't had major direct issues with law enforcement. The most personal thing was getting pulled over once after a late shift because one of my brake lights was out, and it ended up just being a warning. I've also been around police at festivals, traffic accidents, or school situations, but nothing like an arrest or serious case for me. As a Latina, I was raised to stay calm, have your paperwork ready, and not make anything harder than it has to be.

follow_ups.question: How did you feel during that traffic stop?
follow_ups.response: Nervous at first because it was dark and I was alone, but the officer was brief and professional.

follow_ups.question: Did that change how you think about police at all?
follow_ups.response: It mostly just reminded me how vulnerable a simple stop can feel when you're a young woman alone at night.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly seeing police around community events or after fender-benders. I also remember school resource officers being around campus when I was younger, and that always made school feel a little more tense than it needed to.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever talk with school officers directly?
follow_ups.response: Only in basic passing ways, nothing serious.

follow_ups.question: What made the atmosphere feel tense?
follow_ups.response: Just having that authority presence there all the time made normal teenage stuff feel more loaded.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No arrests in my immediate family or for me. I do have a cousin who got a DUI a few years ago, and that scared everybody because it was so avoidable.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect how your family talks about drinking and driving?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, very directly—now it comes up at family parties all the time.

follow_ups.question: Was your cousin okay in the end?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, it was more a wake-up call than a tragedy, thankfully.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I started voting as soon as I was eligible, and I've voted in the 2024 general and the most recent primary. I wouldn't say I'm the most perfect voter who knows every tiny local race deeply, but I do take it seriously and try not to skip. I especially pay attention when issues touch education, healthcare, immigration, workers, or cost of living because those feel real in my life. Sometimes I still need time to research the local judges and propositions because those can be confusing.

follow_ups.question: How do you usually decide who or what to vote for?
follow_ups.response: I read voter guides, look up nonpartisan summaries, and talk with people I trust before I fill things out.

follow_ups.question: Do you usually vote by mail or in person?
follow_ups.response: By mail mostly, because it's easier for me with work.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I lean pretty clearly left, but I think of myself as practical before ideological. I care a lot about affordable education, healthcare access, reproductive freedom, immigrant dignity, workers getting paid fairly, and housing costs because those are not abstract issues where I come from. Being in service work also makes me pay attention to how power works—who gets listened to, who gets protected, and who gets treated like they're disposable. I believe government should actually help ordinary people, not just tell them to work harder while everything keeps getting more expensive. At the same time, I get frustrated with political talk that feels performative or disconnected from everyday life, because if a policy sounds good but nobody can access it or understand it, that matters too. So I guess I'd describe myself as a young Latina Democrat who wants compassion, accountability, and things that actually function.

follow_ups.question: Are there issues that feel especially personal for you?
follow_ups.response: Education and healthcare are big ones, and also immigration because even if my own story is U.S.-born, that issue touches so many people I love.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics much with your family?
follow_ups.response: Some, yes, but usually in a practical way—rent, schools, wages, not like all-day cable-news arguments.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I've gotten more engaged with local and everyday policy stuff as I've gotten older. When I was younger, politics felt like something loud and far away, but now I notice how city decisions, school options, minimum wage, healthcare rules, and transportation affect daily life. I've also become more skeptical of people posting politics just for aesthetics without doing much in real life. So my values haven't totally changed, but they've gotten more concrete and less vague.

follow_ups.question: Was there something specific that made politics feel more real?
follow_ups.response: Work and money, honestly—once you're paying bills and trying to get back into school, policy stops feeling theoretical.

follow_ups.question: Have your views become stronger or just more informed?
follow_ups.response: More informed and a little stronger.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They've affected me a fair amount. I'm not Black, so I try not to center myself in that, but being a woman of color in public-facing jobs means I notice how race shapes who gets treated with patience, who gets watched, and who gets believed. I also have coworkers and friends from different backgrounds, and hearing their stories made the issue feel very human and close. So I would say it affected me both through empathy and through paying more attention to systems I maybe didn't have language for before.

follow_ups.question: Did anything at work make that clearer to you?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, just seeing how some customers speak differently to staff depending on who they're talking to.

follow_ups.question: Did those conversations happen in your family too?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though my parents sometimes frame it more cautiously because they worry about safety and conflict.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I've been thinking about accountability, dignity, and what safety really means. A lot of people say they want safety, but if some communities are constantly over-policed or not treated like their lives matter equally, that isn't real safety to me. I've also thought more about how race intersects with class, neighborhood, school discipline, and jobs. For me the biggest thing is listening, not acting like one social media post means you've done the work.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed how you move through public spaces?
follow_ups.response: It made me more observant and more likely to notice unfair treatment in the moment.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel hopeful about change?
follow_ups.response: Some days yes, especially with younger people, but I also think progress can be fragile.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is still built into a lot more of American life than people like to admit. It shows up in schools, where neighborhoods get resources, in healthcare, in who gets grace when they make a mistake, and in service jobs too. Growing up in Orange County, I was always around different communities, so I saw both multicultural beauty and quiet segregation at the same time. Recently I've been trying to think about race less like a one-time headline and more like a daily structure.

follow_ups.question: Does being bilingual affect how you see that?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because language changes how people treat you too—sometimes positively, sometimes like they assume things about you.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about race with friends more than with family?
follow_ups.response: Usually yes, just because friends tend to use more direct language about it.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: Mostly I've talked with family and friends, shared information, and paid more attention to local organizations and artists speaking on these issues. I also went to a peaceful community event in Santa Ana that mixed art and discussion around justice, which felt more like me than arguing online.

follow_ups.question: Why did that kind of event fit you better?
follow_ups.response: Because art makes conversation feel more human and grounded for me.

follow_ups.question: Do you post much about these issues?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but not constantly—I try not to post more than I'm willing to learn or act.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My close friends are generally pretty engaged and talk openly about it. My parents care, but their style is more cautious and private—they come from a place of 'be aware, stay safe, don't invite trouble,' which I understand. My brother gets a lot of this through school and social media, so his generation talks about it more directly. At work, I've heard a wide range, from people who are very thoughtful to people who just want to avoid the topic completely.

follow_ups.question: Have these differences caused conflict?
follow_ups.response: Not major conflict, more like different comfort levels and ways of expressing concern.

follow_ups.question: Who do you feel most aligned with?
follow_ups.response: Probably my friends, though I understand where my parents are coming from too.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall, I'd say my health is pretty good. I'm active, I do yoga, run, hike, and play beach volleyball sometimes, and I try to eat decently even though restaurant work makes that tricky. I do get seasonal allergies, tension headaches if I'm dehydrated or stressed, and sometimes my stomach feels off if I drink too much coffee on an empty stomach. I also get pretty painful period cramps some months, but nothing I've been told is a major condition.

follow_ups.question: Do you usually see a doctor regularly?
follow_ups.response: Basic checkups, yes, though I'm less on top of dental than I should be.

follow_ups.question: How's your sleep?
follow_ups.response: Decent when my schedule is stable, but late shifts and homework can throw it off.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: What makes it easier is that I genuinely like movement, and living in Southern California means I can hike, run, or go outside most of the year. What makes it harder is money, variable work hours, stress, and food choices when you're around pastries and fries and coffee all day. Also when I'm overwhelmed, routines are the first thing that slip.

follow_ups.question: What's the first healthy habit to go when you're stressed?
follow_ups.response: Sleep and meal timing, usually.

follow_ups.question: What helps you get back on track?
follow_ups.response: A schedule, a walk, and not trying to fix everything in one day.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge or life-changing. Last summer I sprained my ankle playing beach volleyball, and that messed with both work and exercise for a couple weeks because I was trying to host while not putting too much pressure on it. I also had a rough stretch with wisdom tooth pain and ended up needing treatment after putting it off longer than I should have. I had COVID once in the last two years too, but it was mild and mostly felt like a really exhausting flu week.

follow_ups.question: Did the ankle injury keep you out of work?
follow_ups.response: Only briefly—I came back with a brace and tried to be careful.

follow_ups.question: Why did you delay the dental issue?
follow_ups.response: Cost and timing, mostly, plus I kept hoping it would calm down on its own.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: For me it's been more temporary than major. The ankle and the tooth pain made work harder, and when my cramps are bad I can be slower or more tired, but I haven't had a long-term health issue stop me from working.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever had to call out because of health?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but not often.

follow_ups.question: Do you usually push through pain?
follow_ups.response: Probably more than I should, especially if I know the shift is already understaffed.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yeah, that matters too. My grandma has diabetes, so there's always some level of checking in around her food, appointments, and how she's feeling. My mom also has high blood pressure, and stress definitely doesn't help that. It's not like my whole life revolves around caregiving, but family health is always in the background of decisions.

follow_ups.question: Do you help take your grandma to appointments?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, if I have a morning free and my parents are working.

follow_ups.question: Does your mom's blood pressure worry you?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, especially when she's overtired, because she's the kind of person who keeps going no matter what.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: Basic medical care has been mostly manageable because I'm still covered through my dad's insurance, but 'manageable' doesn't mean easy. The harder parts are dental, vision, specialist stuff, and just finding time without losing work hours.
